title: Signal Lifecycle: Who Clears a Flag?
scenario: It is 6:08 AM. The trader's flag was raised in the 5:40 note - and the 6:05 correction never mentions it. Signals have lifecycles: they are raised, they persist, and someone specific clears them. Get the lifecycle wrong and escalations either never end or silently vanish.
input:
[5:40 AM note] "... Trader flagged the spike for review."
[6:05 AM correction] Corrects the settled price. Says nothing about the flag.

Desk agreement on escalation signals: a flag stays active until the role that owns the escalation channel (the Desk Trader) explicitly clears it. When signals conflict - one source escalates, another reads routine - the workflow fails toward review.
instructions: Track the flag across both notes.

questions.prompt: The 6:05 correction does not mention the flag. What is the flag's status?

options.text: Expired - each new note resets all signals
Still active - an unretracted escalation persists
Ambiguous - the workflow should skip approval to be efficient

questions.explain: The desk agreement in the input says a flag stays active until explicitly cleared. Silence about a signal is not a retraction of it.

questions.prompt: Who may clear a raised flag?

options.text: Anyone who reads the note stream
The workflow, automatically, when the brief ships
The role that owns the escalation channel - the Desk Trader

questions.explain: Signals have owners. The input names the owning role; clearing rights follow channel ownership, not readership.

questions.prompt: If one source escalates and another reads routine, which way does the workflow fail?

options.text: Toward review - a possibly-unnecessary approval beats a missed escalation
It halts entirely until a human resolves the conflict

questions.explain: The desk agreement states the fail direction. The two error costs are asymmetric: an extra review wastes minutes; a missed escalation ships an unapproved brief.

questions.prompt: So what value does approvalRequired carry into today's intake record?

options.text: false - the correction superseded everything in the first note
true - the flag was raised and never cleared
null - the second note is silent about it

questions.explain: Later-wins applies to VALUES both notes state (like the settled price). The flag was raised and never cleared by its owner, so it persists - and persistence is a known fact, not a null.

artifactOnPass.lifecycleRule: active until explicitly cleared by the owning role

copilotPrompt: Reason about an escalation signal's lifecycle: does an unmentioned flag persist, who may clear it, which way conflicting signals fail, and what approvalRequired carries today.
successMessage: Lifecycle judged. The flag persists, its owner is known, and the fail direction is on record.

intro.heading: Before you judge: signals have lifecycles

sections.title: Raised, persisting, cleared
sections.body: A signal is not a fact about the world - it is a request with a lifecycle. The easy tier asked what the flag becomes; this tier asks how long it lives and who ends it.

sections.title: Silence is not retraction
sections.body: The correction note fixes a price and says nothing about the flag. Treating silence as clearance is how escalations vanish without anyone deciding they should.

sections.title: Fail direction is a design choice
sections.body: When signals conflict, some workflows fail toward action, some toward review, some halt. The right choice depends on asymmetric error costs - and it must be decided and written down before the conflict happens.

takeaway.heading: Signal lifecycle recorded
points: You distinguished later-wins (for stated values) from persistence (for unretracted signals) - two different rules that both applied this morning.
You located clearing rights with the channel owner, not with whoever reads the note.
You applied the fail-toward-review principle and can say WHY: the error costs are asymmetric.
approvalRequired carries true into the intake record on this tier - and the delegation drama later this morning depends on it.
The workflow can now manage an escalation signal across its whole lifecycle, not just at the moment it is raised.
